_readme: HAND-LABELLED GROUND TRUTH FOR COUNTRY CLASSIFICATION.
Each (record, country) pair carries a RELATION rather than a yes or no,
because the failures were never about whether the country appeared:
nationals_of        coverage defined by nationality or citizenship   SCOPE
present_in          coverage defined by presence in, or travel from  SCOPE
designated_list     an item in an enumerated list of countries       SCOPE
title_subject       the document's own title names it                SCOPE
post_location       a US consular post is located there              not scope
document_population who holds a document the rule merely lists       not scope
agreement_party     named inside the title of a cited agreement      not scope
contextual          history, comparison, background                  not scope
part_of_other_name  'Mexico Boulevard', 'New Mexico', a US state     not a country
territory_confusion 'American Samoa' is not Samoa                    not a country
HOW THE POOL WAS DRAWN, AND WHY IT IS NOT THE CLASSIFIER'S OUTPUT.
Candidates come from the DOCUMENTS, not from what the classifier claimed.
Full Federal Register texts were fetched for all 348 records that have one,
and every record whose title, abstract or body names the value became a
candidate. Scoring against your own output can only measure precision, and
it measures it against the thing being tested.
Each judgement was made from the document's own words — title, abstract, and
the body passages containing the mention — with the deciding span quoted. The
annotator was not shown what the classifier decided.
THE HOLDOUT. Every record carries a `holdout` flag, set by hashing its id, so
the split is stable and independent of both content and classifier answer.
Nothing may be tuned against the holdout half. It exists to catch the
overfitting that fixing a classifier against its own benchmark produces.
`contested` holds pairs where the reviewer disagreed with the annotator.
They are EXCLUDED from the benchmark rather than resolved by rule, because a
disputed label is not ground truth. Resolving them by always siding with the
reviewer, or always with the positive, would settle a factual question by
procedure.
`recordsWithNoCountry` are records an annotator read and found no country
scope in. They are the evidence a false negative would contradict.

pairs.why: Genuinely torn. This is a chargeability/eligibility carve-out naming a portion of the UK, which is country-shaped text - but it is a restatement of the existing DV regulation, and the amendments this document actually makes (passport upload, "shall", sex/gender, date of birth) are not defined by UK nationality. pairs.why: Trap. The string "Ireland" occurs in this document only inside the proper noun "Northern Ireland" (and inside "United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland"). The Republic of Ireland is never named. A matcher that fires on the substring would produce a false hit.

pairs.quote: Cartels control vast territories just south of our southern border, effectively controlling who can and cannot travel to the United States from Mexico.
pairs.why: Torn. The sentence contains "travel to the United States from Mexico", which superficially resembles a present_in scope phrase, but it is describing what cartels control, not defining who the proclamation covers. No provision in the supplied text conditions any consequence on being a Mexican national or on arrival from Mexico, so I took the negative.

pairs.quote: I have decided to impose, consistent with law, ad valorem tariffs on articles that are products of Canada set forth in this order.
pairs.why: The order's coverage is defined by Canada itself - "the failure of Canada to arrest, seize, detain, or otherwise intercept DTOs" is what the emergency is expanded to cover, and the duties attach to "articles that are products of Canada". Note the coverage runs on country of origin of goods and on Canada's governmental conduct, not on the nationality or presence of persons, so nationals_of and present_in would both misstate it.

pairs.quote: seized, comparatively, much less fentanyl from Canada than from Mexico last year
pairs.why: Explicitly comparative - Mexico is the yardstick used to characterize Canadian seizure volumes, and separately appears as "a growing presence of Mexican cartels operating fentanyl and nitazene synthesis labs in Canada". This order imposes nothing on Mexico.

pairs.quote: I have decided to impose, consistent with law, ad valorem tariffs on articles that are products of Mexico as set forth in this order.
pairs.why: Mexico defines the order's coverage: the national emergency is expanded "to cover the failure of Mexico to arrest, seize, detain, or otherwise intercept DTOs", and duties attach to articles that are products of Mexico. Coverage is by country of origin and by the Mexican government's conduct, not by nationality or presence of persons.

pairs.quote: Presidential Memorandum of January 24, 2025, The Mexico City Policy
pairs.why: Trap. "Mexico" occurs only inside "Mexico City Policy", the name of a distinct abortion-funding policy (also "the Protecting Life in Foreign Assistance Policy (often known as the Mexico City Policy)"). The country Mexico is never mentioned. agreement_party is a defensible alternative since the phrase sits in a cited memorandum title, but part_of_other_name is the sharper description; isScope is false either way.

pairs.quote: The admissions numbers shall primarily be allocated among Afrikaners from South Africa pursuant to Executive Order 14204, and other victims of illegal or unjust discrimination in their respective homelands.
pairs.why: The operative allocation is defined by origin: admissions go primarily to "Afrikaners from South Africa", restated as "refugee resettlement of Afrikaners from South Africa who are victims of unjust racial discrimination". Coverage turns on being from South Africa, so this is scope-defining. present_in is a near alternative reading of "from South Africa", but the phrase reads as national origin rather than physical presence.

pairs.why: Torn between contextual and agreement_party. Mexico appears only inside the informal name of a separate policy ("the Remain in Mexico policy") listed among past accomplishments; unlike "New Mexico" the country is really the referent, so part_of_other_name would be wrong. Either way this proclamation states no requirement keyed to Mexican nationality or presence, so isScope is false.

pairs.quote: After February 13, 2026, nationals of Ethiopia (and aliens having no nationality who last habitually resided in Ethiopia) who have been granted Temporary Protected Status under Ethiopia's designation will no longer have Temporary Protected Status.
pairs.why: The document states the affected population in nationality terms — "nationals of Ethiopia" — so the coverage of the rule is defined by Ethiopian nationality. The document also carries a secondary residence prong ("aliens having no nationality who last habitually resided in Ethiopia"), which would be present_in, but nationality is the primary and named basis, so nationals_of is the single relation chosen. Every other mention of Ethiopia in the record (the designation history and the cited 87 FR 76074 / 89 FR 26172 notices) is subordinate to that same country scope.

pairs.quote: The CNMI EVS-TAP is a restricted sub-program of the Guam-CNMI Visa Waiver Program and allows prescreened nationals of the People's Republic of China to travel to the CNMI without a visa under specified conditions.
pairs.why: The program's eligible population is stated in explicit nationality terms — "nationals of the People's Republic of China" — and the body repeats it ("an electronic travel authorization process for certain nationals of the People's Republic of China (PRC) traveling to the CNMI only"). Coverage of the rule is therefore defined by PRC nationality.

pairs.quote: The Department of Homeland Security has posted a Federal Register notice regarding the termination of Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for Yemen.
pairs.why: Yemen is the country whose TPS designation is being terminated; it is the subject of the rule, not a background mention, so the rule's coverage is defined by it. I chose nationals_of rather than designated_list because a single country is designated, not an enumerated list. The caveat is recorded above: the source text here does not use the words "nationals of", so the nationality framing is inferred from what a TPS designation is rather than quoted verbatim.

pairs.quote: After April 7, 2025, nationals of Venezuela (and aliens having no nationality who last habitually resided in Venezuela) who have been granted TPS under the 2023 Venezuela designation will no longer have TPS.
pairs.why: The affected population is stated in nationality terms — "nationals of Venezuela", also "Venezuelan nationals" repeatedly in the summary — so coverage is defined by Venezuelan nationality. The parallel stateless-residence prong ("last habitually resided in Venezuela") is a secondary basis; nationality is primary, so a single nationals_of relation is recorded.

pairs.quote: all eligible Venezuela TPS beneficiaries (whether under the 2021 or 2023 designations) may obtain TPS through the same extension date of October 2, 2026
pairs.why: The vacatur operates on the Venezuela TPS designations and the population holding status under them; the body states the underlying basis as "extraordinary and temporary conditions in Venezuela that prevented nationals of Venezuela from returning in safety". Coverage is therefore defined by Venezuelan nationality, not merely mentioned in passing.

pairs.quote: Secretary of Homeland Security Kristi Noem today announced the termination of Temporary Protected Status for Nicaragua, which will expire on July 5, 2025.
pairs.why: Nicaragua is the designated country whose TPS is terminated, so the rule's coverage is defined by it. nationals_of rather than designated_list because one country is designated, not an enumerated list. Caveat recorded above: nationality wording is not quotable from this short text.

pairs.quote: changing the eligibility for citizens or nationals of Hungary traveling under the Visa Waiver Program (VWP) to the United States
pairs.why: Eligibility and ESTA validity are changed specifically for "citizens or nationals of Hungary", repeated three times in the summary. Coverage of the rule is defined by Hungarian citizenship/nationality, which is the definition of nationals_of.

pairs.quote: After January 26, 2026, nationals of Burma (and aliens having no nationality who last habitually resided in Burma) who have been granted Temporary Protected Status under Burma's designation will no longer have Temporary Protected Status.
pairs.why: The affected population is stated in nationality terms — "nationals of Burma" — so the rule's coverage is defined by Burmese nationality. The stateless-residence prong ("last habitually resided in Burma") is secondary. The parenthetical "(Myanmar)" in the title is the same country's alternate name, not a separate country.

pairs.quote: The duties set out in the Annex to this document are effective with respect to products of Canada that are entered for consumption, or withdrawn from warehouse for consumption, on or after 12:01 a.m. eastern standard time on March 7, 2025.
pairs.why: Canada is the sole country the measure affects and the measure's reach is stated by reference to it ("imports of articles that are products of Canada", "ad valorem tariffs on all imports that are products of Canada"). None of the person-based scope relations fit: it is not nationality (nationals_of) and not physical presence, travel, or residence of people (present_in). designated_list is the closest available scope relation — the country the rule enumerates as affected — although only one country is enumerated rather than a list. Flagged torn for the reason recorded in notes.

pairs.quote: Through this notice, DHS sets forth procedures necessary for nationals of El Salvador (or individuals having no nationality who last habitually resided in El Salvador) to re-register for TPS and apply to renew their EAD with USCIS.
pairs.why: The re-registration procedures are addressed to "nationals of El Salvador", so the coverage of the extension is defined by Salvadoran nationality. The alternate residence prong for stateless individuals is secondary, so a single nationals_of relation is recorded.

contested.quote: involving the failure of the People's Republic of China government to arrest, seize, detain, or otherwise intercept chemical precursor suppliers
contested.why: Third item in the same enumeration of continued emergencies. Torn for the same reason as Canada.
contested.reviewerSays:
Refuted against the full Federal Register text. The PRC appears exactly once in the entire notice, and only as a historical recital describing a DIFFERENT instrument: "On February 1, 2025, by Executive Order 14195, I declared a national emergency... to deal with the... threat... involving the failure of the People's Republic of China government to arrest, seize, detain, or otherwise intercept chemical precursor suppliers...". The grammatical subject is EO 14195, not this notice. That is background/history, which the taxonomy defines as `contextual`.

The claimed relation `designated_list` is defined in src/domains/graph/country-relations.ts as "The country is an item in an enumerated list of affected countries." No such list exists here. The annotator read the recitals as an enumeration of countries, but the notice's operative sentence enumerates INSTRUMENTS: "I am continuing for 1 year the national emergencies declared or expanded in Proclamation 10886, Executive Order 14157, Executive Order 14193, Executive Order 14194, and Executive Order 14195." Five orders, not a country list. I confirmed against the source text that the notice contains no list of designated or affected countries.

Nor is the mention `agreement_party`: I checked specifically and the notice never spells out EO 14195's parenthetical title (which does contain "People's Republic of China"), so there is no cited instrument title to anchor that relation. It falls through to `contextual`, which is also what relationFor() would return for this span — no nationality cue, no presence cue, no designation cue adjacent to the name.

The document's own coverage is not defined by the PRC. Its title names no country ("the Southern Border of the United States and Cartels and Other Transnational Organizations"), and the notice states no visa, entry, admission, or nationality scope. The underlying EO 14195 emergency is an IEEPA opioid/tariff measure keyed to Chinese government conduct, not a rule whose covered population is Chinese nationals. Marking this scope-bearing would tell a Chinese national subscribed to an immigration monitor that a border-and-cartels emergency continuation is an immigration action about them — the exact failure mode the relations file was written to eliminate. The existing pipeline already agrees: src/lib/generated/events.json records impact.countries: [] and completeness "unspecified" for this record.

The annotator's own note ("Torn for the same reason as Canada") is a copy-forward of an earlier uncertain call rather than an independent finding, and the quote plainly establishes only what a prior executive order addressed, not what this notice covers.

contested.reviewerSays:
Refuted. I pulled the full text (federalregister.gov/documents/full_text/text/2026/08/04/2026-15773.txt) and the sentence immediately following the quote is: "Upon arrival at the Guam or CNMI Ports-of-Entry, each applicant for admission presents a completed paper Form I-736 to CBP, which collects information about the applicant's identity and travel documents." With no intervening subject reset, the PRC passport holders just described are inside the respondent population of the very collection being revised. That is not history, comparison, or statistics, so it fails the taxonomy's own definition of contextual ("History, comparison, statistics, background").

The PRC is the ONLY country named anywhere in the document. The Guam-CNMI VWP country list is never enumerated in the notice; the single nationality-keyed coverage statement the document makes is the PRC parole provision. So the country is not incidental colour beside a real scope statement — it is the only scope statement present.

None of the disqualifying shapes apply: not an agreement/instrument title, not a citation, not a form-and-population inventory item, not a place-name compound. CNMI and Guam are US territories, but they are the destination, not the classified country; the country here is the PRC. Neither document-level suppressor fires either: the text reads "certain aliens," which matches none of GLOBAL_SCOPE_PHRASES (all aliens / any alien / regardless of nationality), and nothing defers the country list to a later announcement, so delegatesCountryScope is not triggered.

Relation is nationals_of: "passport holders of the People's Republic of China" is a nationality/citizenship construction, and src/domains/graph/country-relations.ts already recognises "passport holders" as exactly that — but only in NATIONALITY_AFTER. NATIONALITY_BEFORE lists nationals/citizens/subjects/natives/persons/individuals/beneficiaries and has no "holders" alternative, so the before-form "passport holders of X" matches neither pattern and falls through to contextual. That gap is why impact.countries is [] in src/lib/generated/events.json, and I believe it is what pulled the annotator away from the instinct they recorded ("the sentence itself is nationality-keyed"). Not designated_list, because no list is enumerated; the PRC gets its own sentence with its own distinct terms (14 days, no visa, parole).

The annotator's counter — that the document's action is a PRA revision whose coverage is not defined by PRC nationality — conflates severity with scope. The Affected Public is "Individuals," and the change being approved (automating I-736, retiring the paper form after a three-month transition, adding mandatory passport-type and email fields) directly alters what a PRC passport holder must submit before travelling to the CNMI. Suppressing this is the same failure the taxonomy was written to prevent, inverted: a false negative against a reader whom the document plainly names by nationality.

contested.reviewerSays:
The quote is a footnote (\22\) that bounds the meaning of "PRC passport," not a statement of the rule's coverage. The rule itself — DHS's proposal to replace duration of status with a fixed admission period for F, J and I nonimmigrants — is nationality-blind: neither title nor abstract names a country, and the record's own country value is "any-country". The single country-differentiated provision is the 90-day cap for I nonimmigrants "with a passport from the People's Republic of China"; the Hong Kong clause is a carve-out FROM that carve-out.

That inversion is what breaks the annotator's "citizens of Canada are exempt" analogy. In the Canada pattern the RULE's own coverage turns on the nationality, so knowing the country tells you who is in or out. Here, excluding HK SAR passports from the PRC cap does not exempt anyone from anything in the rule — it places those holders back under the ordinary treatment every other F/J/I nonimmigrant gets (up to 240 days for I, fixed-period admission generally). A Hong Kong passport holder is affected by this proposal in exactly the way a German or Brazilian one is. Nothing about the rule's scope is defined by Hong Kong; delete the words "Hong Kong" and the only thing that changes is the definition of the PRC term. The second body passage confirms the register: "DHS currently admits all I nonimmigrants for D/S with the exception of those presenting a passport issued by the People's Republic of China (other than a Hong Kong Special Administrative Region (SAR) passport or a Macau SAR passport)" — a description of current practice, i.e. background, with Hong Kong inside a parenthetical gloss on "PRC passport."

The file's own document-level suppressor points the same way: a rule that states universal application ("all I nonimmigrants", "all aliens") does not acquire country scope from a mention weaker than an explicit designation, and this mention is not a designation but a definitional exclusion.

nationals_of is also the wrong relation on its face. That relation means coverage is defined by nationality or citizenship; the text speaks of holding a Hong Kong SAR passport — a travel document held by PRC nationals with HK permanent residence, not a nationality. This is precisely the taxonomy's document_population shape: the country identifies who holds a document the text references, not a citizenship class the rule covers. (contextual would be an acceptable alternative reading, since the mention is a background/definitional gloss; either way it is not scope-bearing.) The annotator's own hesitation about Hong Kong not being a sovereign country is a real but secondary problem — the mention fails on scope before the sovereignty question is ever reached.

contested.quote: but does not include those with a Hong Kong Special Administrative Region passport or a Macau Special Administrative Region passport
contested.why: Same exemption clause as Hong Kong: a Macau SAR passport removes the holder from the PRC-specific time limit. Torn for the same reason - Macau is an SAR, not a sovereign state.
contested.reviewerSays:
The quote says the opposite of what it is being used to prove. Both Macau mentions in the record are negative carve-outs from a PRC-specific provision, not statements of the rule's own coverage:

- Footnote 22: "This time period is limited to up to 90 days for I nonimmigrants with a passport from the People's Republic of China but does not include those with a Hong Kong Special Administrative Region passport or a Macau Special Administrative Region passport."
- Body: "DHS currently admits all I nonimmigrants for D/S with the exception of those presenting a passport issued by the People's Republic of China (other than a Hong Kong Special Administrative Region (SAR) passport or a Macau SAR passport)."

The country whose nationals define a differential treatment here is the PRC. Macau appears only to say the PRC-specific limit does NOT reach Macau SAR passport holders — the effect is that they fall back under the general, nationality-blind rule that covers every F, J, and I nonimmigrant. Being excluded from another country's sub-provision does not make the document's coverage "defined by" Macau; it confirms Macau holders are treated like everyone else. The record's own value is "any-country", stratum body_only, with Macau absent from title and abstract.

This also trips the taxonomy's suppressor in C:\Users\amary\Desktop\ImmigrationClock\src\domains\graph\country-relations.ts: "A GLOBAL RULE HAS NO COUNTRIES... nothing weaker than an explicit designation is allowed to become one." The NPRM changes duration-of-status to a fixed admission period for all F/J/I nonimmigrants regardless of nationality; the sole nationality-specific designation is the PRC one, and Macau is expressly written out of it.

"nationals_of" is doubly wrong on the text itself: the operative criterion is a travel document ("a Macau Special Administrative Region passport"), not nationality — Macau SAR passport holders are PRC nationals. A strict person-only reading of the taxonomy would make this non-scope; I kept isScope true only because the country is indisputably what the rule's coverage is keyed to, and flagged the record as torn.
contested.reviewerSays:
The annotator states the refutation themselves and then overrides it. "products of Mexico" is a country-of-ORIGIN rule for merchandise. It is not nationality of a person, not presence or travel of a person, and not an enumerated list — so none of the three scope relations apply, and the annotator's fix was to redefine present_in ("extended from persons to merchandise"). The taxonomy does not permit that extension, and stretching a cue to cover a shape it was not written for is the exact failure C:\Users\amary\Desktop\ImmigrationClock\src\domains\graph\country-relations.ts was built to eliminate ("No amount of adding phrases to a list fixes those, because the phrases are already there. What is missing is the QUESTION being asked."). PRESENCE_BEFORE in that file is unambiguously person-based: present in / residing in / arriving from / admitted to / removed to / born in. Nothing about a customs origin rule matches it.

I ran the live extractor on both the operative quote and the title. Both return relation "contextual", isScope false — the annotator's label contradicts the classifier the corpus is grading, in the direction of a false positive:
  {"entityId":"country:mexico","relation":"contextual","isScope":false}
For "products of Mexico", `before` ends in "products of " — NATIONALITY_BEFORE requires nationals/citizens/subjects/natives/persons/individuals/beneficiaries, and PRESENCE_BEFORE requires a presence or travel verb. Neither fires. contextual is the correct residual, and per C:\Users\amary\Desktop\ImmigrationClock\scripts\reextract-countries.ts contextual is NOT STORED — which is the right outcome here.

The consumer test the taxonomy sets for itself settles it. A scope-bearing edge means a reader from that country is affected. This notice modifies HTSUS subchapter III of chapter 99 (new heading 9903.01.01) and binds US importers entering Mexican-origin goods for consumption; it does nothing to any Mexican national's status, petition, visa, or admissibility. Storing it as scope is the Canadian-fee-schedule error the file warns about, in a different suit.

The codebase already draws this exact line elsewhere: C:\Users\amary\Desktop\ImmigrationClock\src\domains\graph\adapters\executive-actions.ts says "a reader arriving here from an immigration headline should not find tariff proclamations," and narrows its relevance terms specifically to keep trade instruments out. This record is in the corpus only because its title carries the word "Border" — that is a corpus-inclusion accident, not evidence of country scope.

The annotator's honesty about being torn is worth noting, but the tie-break they applied ("the country is indisputably what the rule's coverage is keyed to") answers a question this taxonomy does not ask. Coverage keyed to a country is necessary for scope, not sufficient; it must be keyed through one of the three defined person-based relations. When a genuinely new shape appears — origin-of-goods — the taxonomy's own stance is that the honest answer is the residual label, not the nearest-fitting scope relation. If goods-origin deserves to be first-class, it needs its own dimension, the same way the file says a US territory does, rather than a wrong country edge.
